s: Welcome to Word Kitchen, the show where we cook up the words you need for real life.
Today we're talking tech, the language of modern work.
Whether you write code or not, these ten words are everywhere.
Tech vocabulary has escaped the office and moved into everyday conversation.
To disrupt means to completely change an industry by introducing something new.
The classic example is how streaming services disrupted television.
The whole business model just collapsed.
One device disrupted cameras, paper maps, alarm clocks, even flashlights.
A small startup disrupts a comfortable market, the giants panic, and within a few years everyone is copying the newcomer.
That's why investors are always hunting for the next disruptor.
They want to fund the company that will disrupt the disruptors.
There is a personal angle too.
Sometimes a new habit disrupts your routine in a good way.
My morning run disrupted my habit of scrolling news in bed, and I feel much better for it.
The trick is to be the one doing the disrupting, not the one being disrupted.
In technology it means data capacity, but in office life it means your mental capacity.
"I don't have the bandwidth for that right now." It's the polite professional way to say I'm completely overwhelmed.
Managers love asking about your bandwidth.
What they really mean is, can I give you one more project?
After our big product launch last spring, my bandwidth was gone for a full week.
I just stared at my screen.
If you don't protect your bandwidth, burnout is not a question of if, it's a question of when.
I started blocking focus time on my calendar.
It gave me my bandwidth back.
Guard your bandwidth like you guard your money, because once it's spent, it's gone.
That means using game-like elements, points, badges, streaks, leaderboards, in activities that are not games.
My running app is pure gamification.
I ran in the rain last Tuesday just to keep my three month streak alive.
It hijacks the part of your brain that loves rewards and progress bars.
Schools are deep into the gamification of learning now.
Kids earn badges for finishing math drills and unlock levels for reading books.
And companies use gamification for training.
Finish the safety course, earn a gold star, climb the leaderboard.
If the points are meaningless, people see through it fast.
Good gamification makes genuine effort feel fun.
Bad gamification is just a sticker on a boring task.
Simply put, it's the level of detail in your data or information.
"We need more granularity in this report." Translation: this summary is too vague.
The right granularity depends on the decision.
A CEO needs the big picture.
An engineer debugging a crash needs the finest detail.
And too much granularity can paralyze a team.
You can analyze forever and never decide.
I learned that the hard way.
I once spent two weeks adding granularity to a dashboard nobody ever opened.
So the rule is, zoom in for granularity, then zoom out before you act.
A beautiful word that means to deliberately make something unclear or hard to understand.
Legal contracts are designed to obfuscate the real price.
Page forty-seven, paragraph nine, surprise fees.
My favorite example is corporate language.
"We're rightsizing the team" is a fancy way to obfuscate a painful truth: people are losing their jobs.
Or when a product page says "pricing tailored to your needs." That usually obfuscates the fact that it's very expensive.
Jargon can obfuscate even a simple idea.
If someone can't explain it in plain words, they might be hiding something.
My personal rule: never obfuscate bad news.
Say it clearly, say it early, and people will respect you for it.
The idea that working together creates something bigger than the sum of the parts.
The synergy between design and engineering is where truly great products are born.
Synergy is also the most abused buzzword in business.
Every merger promises synergy, and very few deliver it.
Real synergy needs shared goals and honest communication.
Without that, it's just a pretty word on a slide.
Remote work created surprising synergy during the pandemic.
Teams collaborated across time zones in ways nobody expected.
I felt that on our team.
The synergy between our writers and our developers made the launch so much stronger.
In tech, it means to officially retire an old tool or system while it still technically works.
"We're going to deprecate the old dashboard next quarter." Translation: stop using it, it's going away.
It means unsupported, unmaintained, living on borrowed time.
When a big platform deprecates a popular feature, developers everywhere panic.
Migration is never as smooth as promised.
The respectful way to deprecate something is slowly.
Warn loudly, give people months to adjust, then switch it off.
Companies that deprecate overnight earn a special kind of hatred from their users.
The silent enemy of every video call.
High latency is why your colleague freezes mid-sentence on a call.
You nod politely at a frozen face.
In competitive gaming, a delay of a few milliseconds decides who wins and who loses.
That's why companies spend millions fighting latency.
Faster servers, data centers closer to users, cables across the ocean floor.
That awkward pause before someone answers a difficult question in a meeting.
Low latency communication, fast clear answers, builds enormous trust in a team.
The narrow point in a process where everything slows down.
On our team, approvals were the bottleneck.
One manager, fifty requests, total gridlock for weeks.
The tricky thing about a bottleneck is that fixing one often reveals another.
Before you scale anything, find the bottleneck.
Pushing more traffic through a narrow pipe just creates a bigger jam.
Smart teams remove the bottleneck instead of adding pressure.
Automate the slow step, or give it more people.
Find the bottleneck and fix the system.
Doing things in small repeated steps, improving a little each time.
Take an iterative approach to everything.
Great software is iterative by nature.
Nobody ships a perfect product on day one.
I'm iterative with my personal habits too.
One small improvement a week beats a giant resolution every January.
Iterative feedback loops are the real secret.
The faster you learn from real users, the faster you improve.
And being iterative takes the pressure off.
You just need the next small step.
Let's do a quick recap, rapid fire.
To disrupt is to shake up an entire industry with something new.
Bandwidth is your mental capacity to take on more work.
Gamification turns ordinary tasks into games with points and badges.
Granularity is the level of detail in your information.
To obfuscate is to deliberately make something confusing.
Synergy is the magic that happens when a team truly works as one.
To deprecate is to politely retire old technology.
Latency is the delay we all hate, from video calls to slow answers.
A bottleneck is the narrow point where all progress gets stuck.
And iterative means improving step by step, forever.
This week, use these words in real life.
Tell your manager about your bandwidth.
Spot the bottleneck in your team's process.
And when a contract tries to obfuscate the price, or a meeting lacks synergy, you'll have the exact word for it.
I'll be the manager, you be the engineer.
I don't have the bandwidth to take on the new dashboard this sprint.
Is it the design work or the data?
The analytics team won't give me the right granularity.
I keep asking for detail and they send me summaries.
Tell you what, let's take an iterative approach.
Ship a simple version first, then add detail later.
And can we deprecate the old reporting tool while we're at it?
The latency on it is terrible.
Ten advanced words, one normal conversation.
Use them until they feel like yours.
These ten words will make you sound sharper in any tech conversation.
